concepts.name: Mechanical equilibrium and local oscillation about equilibrium
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite foundation owned by kinematics and dynamics (Topic 2 and Topic 3); a particle displaced from rest experiences restoring interactions and oscillates locally across its equilibrium position.
misconceptions: Assuming an oscillating particle must have a permanent net displacement after completing a cycle of motion.
Confusing the temporary displacement of a particle from rest with a permanent relocation of that particle.
demands: Recall that the equilibrium position is the undisturbed resting position of a particle.
Recall that oscillation is repetitive back-and-forth motion around an equilibrium position.

concepts.name: Work done, kinetic energy, and potential energy transfer in mechanical systems
concepts.why_this_depth: Prerequisite foundation owned by Topic 5 (Work, energy and power); work done by an external source imparts kinetic and elastic potential energy to matter.
misconceptions: Conflating energy transfer with the physical transport of mass across space.
Assuming mechanical energy cannot pass along a medium unless the material particles travel to the final destination.
demands: Recall that work done on an object or medium transfers energy to that system.
Recall that moving particles possess kinetic energy and displaced elastic elements possess potential energy.

concepts.name: Wave motion as a travelling disturbance via neighbour interactions
concepts.why_this_depth: Directly carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m01_o01; establishes the foundational mechanism of wave propagation where an initial disturbance propagates through inter-element forces.
misconceptions: Believing that a wave is a physical object or stream of matter flowing continuously through space.
Believing that particles in a medium must travel along with the wave disturbance from source to receiver.
Assuming that a disturbance can travel through a mechanical medium without any physical interactions or coupling between adjacent sections.
demands: Describe wave motion as the propagation of a disturbance through a medium or space.
Explain how an initial displacement of one section of a medium causes forces on adjacent sections, transmitting the disturbance progressively from neighbour to neighbour.
Identify that individual particles or sections of the medium oscillate locally about their equilibrium positions while the disturbance advances.

concepts.name: Mechanical illustrations of wave motion in ropes, springs, and ripple tanks
concepts.why_this_depth: Specifically mandated by syllabus learning outcome 9702_t07_m01_o01; students must describe wave motion as illustrated across these three physical apparatuses.
misconceptions: Believing water in a ripple tank is transported en masse from a vibrating paddle across the tank to the far wall.
Believing that individual coils of a stretched spring migrate to the far end when a compression pulse travels along it.
Believing a marker or ribbon tied to a rope travels to the far end with an advancing pulse.
demands: Describe how flicking one end of a stretched rope sends a pulse along the rope while a marked point moves perpendicularly and returns to equilibrium.

Describe how pushing and pulling the end of a stretched spring sends a compression or rarefaction pulse along the spring while individual coils oscillate along the spring axis and return to equilibrium.
Describe how a vibrating dipper in a ripple tank produces circular or straight wavefronts that spread across the surface while a floating cork or surface water element bobs locally about equilibrium.
Compare the three systems to show the common physical principle: a travelling pattern of disturbance combined with local, bounded oscillation of the medium.

concepts.name: Progressive waves and energy transfer without net matter transport
concepts.why_this_depth: Carries owned outcome 9702_t07_m01_o06 and official definition 9702_def_progressive_wave; directly tested across Cambridge examinations (9702_s25_24_q04_a_i, 9702_w17_21_q03_a_i, 9702_s22_12_q21, 9702_s17_12_q23).
misconceptions: Omitting energy transfer from the definition of a progressive wave (such as defining it merely as a moving shape).
Believing that progressive waves carry matter from source to receiver.
Thinking that because medium particles return to their initial resting positions after a wave passes, no energy was transferred.
Assuming progressive waves have permanently stationary nodes with zero amplitude.
demands: State the verbatim definition of a progressive wave: a wave that transfers energy from place to place.
Explain that progressive waves transfer energy from a source to a receiver without causing any net transfer of the medium.
Identify physical observations that provide evidence of energy arrival at a distant point (such as movement of a distant ring, vibration of an absorber, or bobbing of a floating object).
State the fundamental distinction between progressive waves (which transfer energy along the wave) and stationary waves (which do not transfer energy along the wave).

concepts.name: Two-track wave analysis: disturbance propagation versus local particle oscillation
concepts.why_this_depth: Essential conceptual discriminator for understanding wave kinematics before formal mathematical definitions in lesson 2; tested in 9702_s22_21_q05_d and P1 questions.
misconceptions: Confusing the constant speed of wave propagation with the varying velocity of an oscillating particle.
Believing that when a particle momentarily reaches zero speed at maximum displacement, the wave itself stops moving.
Confusing the direction of wave travel with the direction of particle motion.
demands: Separate wave analysis into two distinct tracks: (1) the speed and direction of the travelling disturbance, and (2) the displacement, velocity, and restoring forces of an individual particle of the medium.
Explain that the disturbance advances at a constant propagation speed while particles accelerate, decelerate, and reverse direction about their equilibrium positions.
Deduce that over an integer number of full cycles or after a pulse passes, the net displacement of any medium particle is zero.

concepts.name: Continuous periodic wave trains versus single travelling pulses
concepts.why_this_depth: Required to bridge isolated single-pulse demonstrations (ropes, springs) to continuous wave phenomena tested in Cambridge questions (such as continuous ripples in tanks and vibration generators).
misconceptions: Believing that a single pulse is governed by completely different physical principles than a continuous wave.
Believing all particles along a wave train move in unison with identical instantaneous displacements.
demands: Explain that a single disturbance produces a travelling pulse, whereas a continuous, repeated oscillation of a source produces a continuous train of waves.
Explain that in a continuous progressive wave train, successive particles along the direction of propagation repeat the source motion with a progressive delay.

concepts.name: Mechanical waves requiring a material medium versus electromagnetic waves in a vacuum
concepts.why_this_depth: Contextual broadening tested in MCQ distractors (such as 9702_s22_12_q21 option C); students must know that while ropes, springs, and water require particles, progressive waves also include light and microwaves which propagate through a vacuum.
misconceptions: Believing that all progressive waves require material particles to propagate.
Believing electromagnetic waves are not progressive waves because they do not have material particles.
demands: Mention that waves in ropes, springs, water, and sound are mechanical waves requiring a material medium of particles.
Mention that progressive waves also include electromagnetic waves (such as light and microwaves) which transfer energy without requiring any material medium and can travel through a vacuum.

hook.historical_investigation: Leonardo da Vinci (c. 1500 - 1510) and his investigation of wave motion in wind-blown wheat fields and water surfaces in Manuscript A and the Codex Leicester.
hook.why_this_spine: Leonardo was the first natural philosopher to isolate the fundamental physical principle that wave motion is the propagation of a disturbance and energy across space rather than the physical transport of matter. By observing wind sweeping across a wheat field near Florence, he recognized that an advancing wave pattern travels across the entire field while individual wheat stalks remain rooted in their soil positions, oscillating and returning to the vertical. He connected this to the concentric circular ripples on a pond caused by a dropped stone, where the wave flees outward from the source while floating straws and the water itself merely bob locally up and down. This directly establishes the core syllabus puzzle: how a progressive wave transfers energy from place to place without transferring the medium.

verified_facts.fact: In circa 1500 to 1508 in Florence and Milan, Italian polymath Leonardo da Vinci (1452 - 1519) recorded detailed observations and sketches on the dynamics of water, waves, and fluid flow in his notebooks (notably Manuscript A, Institut de France, and the Codex Leicester).
verified_facts.source: MacCurdy, E. (1938), The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci, Reynal & Hitchcock, Book II: Movement and Weight; Richter, J. P. (1883), The Literary Works of Leonardo da Vinci, Sampson Low.

verified_facts.fact: In Manuscript A (fol. 59r), Leonardo recorded the classic analogy comparing water waves to waves in a wheat field: 'The impetus is much quicker than the water, for it often happens that the wave flees the place of its creation, while the water does not; like the waves made in a field of grain by the wind, where we see the waves running across the field while the grain remains in place.'
verified_facts.source: Leonardo da Vinci, Manuscript A (Institut de France, MS 2172), fol. 59r; Pierce, J. R. (1974), Almost All About Waves, MIT Press, Chapter 1.

verified_facts.fact: Leonardo observed that when a stone falls into calm water, concentric circular ripples spread outward across the surface of the pond, but a floating piece of straw or drop of water does not travel outward with the wave crest; it merely rises and falls locally as the wave passes.
verified_facts.source: MacCurdy, E. (1938), The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci, Section on The Nature of Water; Truesdell, C. (1968), Essays in the History of Mechanics, Springer-Verlag.

verified_facts.fact: Leonardo deduced that waves represent the transmission of an impetus (motion and energy) from one element of the medium to the next through contact pressure, rather than the bulk transport of the water itself across space.
verified_facts.source: Dijksterhuis, E. J. (1961), The Mechanization of the World Picture, Oxford University Press, Part IV.

hook.closing_question: When an observable wave travels across a rope, a spring, or the surface of a pond, what is actually moving across space from the source to the receiver if the physical substance itself remains in place?

activities.reasoning_step: Distinguishing the motion of a travelling disturbance from the local oscillation of a marked medium element in a mechanical system.
misconceptions_addressed: Believing a marked point or piece of material travels along the medium with the wave pattern.
Assuming a marked point remains completely stationary when the disturbance arrives.

activities.reasoning_step: Comparing the direction of local particle oscillation relative to the direction of wave energy propagation across rope, spring, and ripple tank contexts.
misconceptions_addressed: Believing water is transported en masse from a wave source to the boundaries of a tank.
Assuming spring coils travel to the far end of the spring when a compression pulse is sent.

activities.reasoning_step: Identifying the physical quantity transferred from source to receiver by a progressive wave and selecting valid physical evidence for that transfer.
misconceptions_addressed: Thinking progressive waves transport matter across space alongside energy.
Concluding that zero net displacement of medium particles implies zero energy transfer.

activities.reasoning_step: Contrasting the constant forward propagation speed of a wavefront with the variable, reversing velocity of an individual medium particle.
misconceptions_addressed: Conflating the speed of the wave pattern with the instantaneous speed of a vibrating particle.
Believing that when a particle is momentarily at rest at maximum displacement, the wave pattern has also stopped moving.

activities.reasoning_step: Ordering the sequential arrival and local phase responses of successive spaced particles as a continuous wave train propagates along a medium.
misconceptions_addressed: Believing all particles in a medium move simultaneously in the same direction when a progressive wave travels through it.
Believing a single pulse cannot transfer energy like a continuous wave.

activities.reasoning_step: Evaluating hypothetical experimental observations of a floating object on water to deduce whether energy has been transferred and whether net transport of water has occurred.
misconceptions_addressed: Assuming a progressive wave must bodily carry floating objects to the distant edge of the tank.
Assuming that stationary wave features (such as nodes with permanently zero amplitude) are present in an unreflected progressive wave.
